modules.description: Describe where you live and who lives nearby.

grammar.title: Upstairs / Downstairs (在 + 楼上/楼下)
grammar.simpleExplanation: You already know 在 (zài) means 'is located at.' Now pair it with location words to say exactly where something is inside a building: 楼上 (lóushàng, upstairs) and 楼下 (lóuxià, downstairs). Just like 在这儿/在那儿, the location word slots right after 在: 我家在楼上 = My home is upstairs.

visualExamples.note: 楼下 slots right after 在, exactly like 这儿/那儿 did

visualExamples.romanization: Nǐ de gōngyù zài lóushàng ma?

grammar.title: There Is / There Are (有 for Existence)
grammar.simpleExplanation: 有 (yǒu) usually means 'to have,' but it has another job: saying something exists somewhere. Put the place first, then 有, then what's there: 这儿有一个银行 = There's a bank here (literally 'here has a bank'). To say something does NOT exist somewhere, use 没有 instead of 不有 — 有 is one of the few verbs in Mandarin that's negated with 没, not 不.

visualExamples.note: 有 is negated with 没, not 不 — say 没有, never 不有

grammar.title: Ordering Food (点菜 + 份)
grammar.simpleExplanation: 点菜 (diǎn cài) literally means 'point-at dish' — it's how you say 'order food' in a restaurant. To order a specific dish, use the same pattern you already know from ordering drinks: 要 (yào, want) + number + measure word + dish. For food, the measure word is usually 份 (fèn, a portion/order): 我要一份炒饭 = I'd like a portion of fried rice.

visualExamples.english: I'd like a portion of fried rice.
visualExamples.note: 份 (fèn) is the measure word for a dish/order, just like 杯 is for a cup of a drink

visualExamples.script: 我要一份米饭,不要辣的。

grammar.title: Comparing Things with 比
grammar.simpleExplanation: 比 (bǐ) is how you compare two things in Mandarin — it means 'compared to.' Put it between the two things: A 比 B + adjective = A is more [adjective] than B. 这个比那个好吃 = This is tastier than that (literally 'this compared-to that tasty').

visualExamples.english: This soup is sweeter than that one.
visualExamples.note: 比 sits between the two things being compared, right before the adjective

options: This is as tasty as that.

quiz.prompt: Where does 比 go in a comparison sentence?
options: Between the two things, before the adjective

grammar.title: Do You Have...? (有没有)
grammar.simpleExplanation: 有没有 (yǒu méiyǒu) is another way to ask a yes/no question — instead of adding 吗 to the end, you put the verb 有 right next to its own negative 没有. It's especially natural when asking if a shop has something in stock: 有没有大一点的? = Do you have a bigger one? (literally 'have not-have bigger one').

grammar.title: Too Much! (太...了)
grammar.simpleExplanation: 太...了 (tài...le) wraps around an adjective to mean 'way too [adjective]' — it's how you complain something is excessive. 太贵了 = too expensive. Just sandwich the adjective between 太 and 了: 太 + adjective + 了.

visualExamples.note: Add 不 before 太 to say something ISN'T excessively so

quiz.prompt: Where does the adjective go in 太...了?
